title: Mansur didn't climb for nothing
takeaway: Real love isn't scared of hard times. It walks straight through them.
scene: The poet describes how a true lover lives: with no peace except the beloved, generous to everyone who asks, and unafraid of what love might cost.

original: دردی بن کے کوئی وی درد ونڈاندا نئیں
سجناں باجھوں چین دلے نوں آندا نئیں
transliteration: Dardi ban ke koi vi dard vandaanda nahin
Sajnaan baajhon chain dile nu aanda nahin
translation: No one becomes a friend in pain and shares the hurt.
Without the beloved, the heart finds no peace.
couplets.story: Nobody steps up to share his pain. And without the Beloved, his heart can't settle down.

original: باس جویں آ جاندی دوروں پھلاں دی
دل وچ وسیا پیار لکایا جاندا نئیں
transliteration: Baas jiven aa jaandi dooron phullaan di
Dil vich vasiya pyaar lukaaya jaanda nahin
translation: Just as the scent of flowers reaches you from far away,
love living in the heart can't be hidden.
couplets.story: You can smell flowers from far off, even when you can't see them. Love is the same. When it lives in your heart, it shows, however hard you try to hide it.

original: جگ وچ ہے مشہور سخاوت سوہنے دی
سائل بھر دے کاسے خالی جاندا نئیں
transliteration: Jag vich hai mashhoor sakhaawat sohne di
Saail bhar de kaase, khaali jaanda nahin
translation: The beloved's generosity is famous throughout the world:
they fill the beggar's bowl, and no one goes away empty-handed.
couplets.story: The Beloved is famous everywhere for being generous. Anyone who comes asking gets their bowl filled. No one leaves with nothing. Punjabi poets often speak of the Prophet ﷺ this way: it was said he never turned anyone away.

original: میں سجناں دے پیار سہارے جیناواں
آس میری دا پھل کدی کملاندا نئیں
transliteration: Main sajnaan de pyaar sahaare jeenaa vaan
Aas meri da phull kadi kumlaanda nahin
translation: I live leaning on the beloved's love;
the flower of my hope never wilts.
couplets.story: He lives by leaning on the Beloved's love. Because of it, his hope is like a flower that never dies.

original: ایویں نئیں منصور چڑھ دے سولی تے
عاشق سچا اوکڑ توں گھبراندا نئیں
transliteration: Aiven nahin Mansoor charhde sooli te
Aashiq sachcha aukar ton ghabraanda nahin
translation: Mansurs don't climb the gallows for nothing:
a true lover isn't frightened of hardship.
couplets.story: People like Mansur didn't climb up to the gallows for no reason. They did it because real love isn't scared of hard things, even death.

original: ابرو تیغ کماں نوں تکھے وار کرے
کجھے پھٹ ہے لاوندا رحم کماندا نئیں
transliteration: Abroo tegh kamaan nu tikkhe vaar kare
Kujhe phatt hai laaunda, rahm kamaanda nahin
translation: The brow strikes sharp blows like a sword and a drawn bow;
it leaves a few wounds, and shows no mercy.
couplets.story: The Beloved's eyebrows are shaped like a bow and as sharp as a sword. They hurt him, and they don't hold back.

original: ڈھو سدھراں دا بوہا کنڈی کھولاں تاں
اپنے گل وچ آپ گھلاواں پاندا نئیں
transliteration: Dho sadhraan da boha kundi kholaan taan
Apne gal vich aap ghulaavaan paanda nahin
translation: If I open the latch on the door of my longings,
I won't be the one who puts a noose around my own neck.
couplets.story: If he ever lets out all his longings, he says, at least he won't be the one who causes his own downfall.

original: صدق خلوصوں جیہڑا اک دا ہو جاوے
کدی وی احمدؔ در در ٹھوکر کھاندا نئیں
transliteration: Sidq khuloson jehra ik da ho jaave
Kadi vi Ahmad dar dar thokar khaanda nahin
translation: Whoever belongs to the One, in truth and sincerity,
Ahmad, never stumbles from door to door.
couplets.story: He ends with something simple and strong. If you give yourself sincerely to the One, you'll never have to go begging from door to door.

deeper:
The last couplet is direct: whoever belongs sincerely to 'the One' (ik) is never left begging at other people's doors. In Punjabi Sufi poetry, 'the One' means God. The generous one who never sends a beggar away empty is a picture of God, who answers everyone who asks. It is also how Punjabi na'ats speak of the Prophet ﷺ, the 'sohna', the beautiful one. His companions said he never answered 'no' to anyone who asked him for something (Bukhari).

Mansur appears again as the model of fearless love. His climb to the gallows wasn't madness. It was what sincere love for God looks like when tested.
why: It ends with a line worth memorising: give yourself fully to the One, and you'll never have to beg from anyone else.
prompt: What gives you hope that doesn't wilt, even on hard days?
notes: A second version of this ghazal is printed on page 56; it is kept here as a variant.

variant.summary: A second version of this ghazal is printed on page 56. It shares four couplets with page 35 and adds two of its own, given here.

original: ہوکے ہاڑے سارے پیڑاں دے کے وی
کہندا اے دلدار میں تڑفاندا نئیں
transliteration: Hauke haare saare peeraan de ke vi
Kehnda ae dildaar main tarfaanda nahin
translation: Even after giving me every sob, plea and pain,
my darling says, 'I'm not making you suffer.'
extraCouplets.story: The Beloved has caused him every kind of pain, every sigh and tear, and still says, 'I'm not hurting you.'

original: سرمداں منصوراں دی ایہہ ریت رہی
سچا عاشق سولی توں گھبراندا نئیں
transliteration: Sarmadaan Mansooraan di eh reet rahi
Sachcha aashiq sooli ton ghabraanda nahin
translation: This has always been the way of the Sarmads and Mansurs:
a true lover isn't afraid of the gallows.
extraCouplets.story: People like Sarmad and Mansur, saints who were executed for their love of God, showed the way. A true lover isn't scared of dying for love.

original: ساقی نے اک جام دتا میں رج گیا
در در تے میں احمدؔ دھکے کھاندا نئیں
transliteration: Saaqi ne ik jaam ditta, main raj gaya
Dar dar te main Ahmad dhakke khaanda nahin
translation: The saqi gave me a single cup, and I was satisfied:
Ahmad, I don't get pushed around from door to door.
extraCouplets.story: The saqi gave him just one cup, and it was enough to fill him up for good. Now he never has to go begging at anyone else's door.
